title: India Faces FIFA World Cup 2026 Blackout as China Secures Broadcast Deal
excerpt: With the tournament less than a month away, Indian fans confront the prospect of watching from the sidelines — while NRIs in host nations tune in freely
body:
Less than a month before the 2026 FIFA World Cup kicks off in the United States, Canada, and Mexico, Indian football fans face an extraordinary prospect: they may not be able to watch the tournament at all.

While China Media Group this week finalised a long-term deal covering both the 2026 and 2030 World Cups — reportedly at around $60 million — India remains without a confirmed broadcaster, the result of a pricing standoff between FIFA and Indian media companies that has dragged on for over a year. The situation is now before the Delhi High Court, which has issued notices to the Indian government and Prasar Bharati and scheduled a hearing for May 20.

## A $80 million gap

The impasse is fundamentally financial. FIFA initially valued Indian broadcast rights at $100 million for the 2026 and 2030 cycle — a figure that reflects the organisation's ambition to tap into what it sees as Asia's next great football market. Indian broadcasters see it differently. JioStar, the country's dominant sports platform after the merger of Disney+ Hotstar and JioCinema, reportedly offered $20 million. Sony, the other plausible buyer, is understood to have bid in the $35–60 million range before walking away.

The gap is not merely about football's relative unpopularity in India compared to cricket. It reflects genuine commercial constraints: most World Cup matches will be played in North and Central American time zones, meaning Indian viewers would be watching at 12:30 AM, 3:30 AM, or 6:30 AM IST. Late-night and early-morning slots attract minimal advertising revenue, which makes the economics of a $100 million rights package extremely difficult to justify in a market where a single IPL season commands more eyeballs than the entire World Cup.

## The Doordarshan option

With private broadcasters balking, attention has turned to Doordarshan, India's public broadcaster. A petition before the Delhi High Court argues that the World Cup qualifies as a "sporting event of national importance" and should be available on free-to-air television under constitutional rights provisions. The petitioners invoke Articles 14, 19(1)(a), and 21 of the Indian Constitution.

Doordarshan's sports channel, DD Sports, has historically stepped in for events where commercial deals fall through, though it typically acquires rights at a fraction of what private broadcasters pay. Whether FIFA would accept Doordarshan's terms — or whether the Indian government would subsidise a deal — remains unclear. The Ministry of Information and Broadcasting has not commented publicly.

## The NRI dimension

For the estimated 18 million Indians living abroad, the blackout risk carries a particular irony. NRI football fans in the US, UK, and Canada — the very countries hosting the tournament — will have no trouble watching matches on local networks. But their families back home in Mumbai, Delhi, and Kochi may be left refreshing social media feeds for updates.

The diaspora's relationship with football has deepened considerably over the past decade. Indian fan clubs for Premier League and La Liga teams have mushroomed across American and British cities, and India's own football ecosystem — buoyed by the Indian Super League — has produced a generation of fans who follow the global game with genuine intensity. The World Cup, hosted in US stadiums that are a short drive from major Indian-American population centres, was supposed to be a watershed moment for Indian football engagement.

## FIFA's own-goal

The broadcast crisis is not India's alone. FIFA's negotiations with China, the world's most populous country, were similarly troubled before CMG's deal was struck. At one point, analysts warned that 40 per cent of the world's population — the combined populations of India and China — might not have guaranteed access to the tournament.

FIFA president Gianni Infantino has championed the expanded 48-team, 104-match format as a vehicle for global growth. But the organisation's commercial strategy has been criticised for pricing rights beyond what emerging football markets can bear. A Deloitte report earlier this year cautioned that failing to secure India and China deals could trigger "significant reputational and financial consequences."

## What happens next

The Delhi High Court hearing on May 20 is now the most important date on Indian football's calendar. If the court directs Prasar Bharati to acquire rights — or pressures FIFA to negotiate more flexibly — Indian fans could yet see the World Cup on their screens when the tournament opens on June 11. If not, India, a country of 1.4 billion people with a rapidly growing football culture, will sit out the world's biggest sporting event.

For NRI fans planning watch parties in Houston, New York, and Toronto, it is a reminder of the uneven terrain of global sports broadcasting — and of the gap between FIFA's aspirations and the markets it claims to serve.
